claim: (a) OCA life of St Stephen Milutin: what it says and does not say about marriages, Simonis, canonisation
ref: OCA (Orthodox Church in America), 'Saint Stephen Milutin of Serbia', Lives of the Saints, commemorated 30 October (web page; no print pagination)
quote_en: «Saint Stephen died on October 29, 1320 and was buried at the Bansk monastery. After two years his incorrupt relics were uncovered.»
edition: OCA web page, read 18 Oct 2026 (copyright OCA; 2-sentence quotation)
what_it_says: The OCA life covers his reign (1275-1320), his defence of Orthodoxy, his 40+ churches and monasteries, his death on 29 October 1320, and the uncovering of his relics two years later. It says NOTHING about his marriages, his wives, Simonis/Simonida, the Byzantine emperor's daughter, any Church objection or dispensation, and it gives no date or act of canonisation (only the heading 'Commemorated on October 30').
limits: A short devotional summary, so its silence proves nothing about the marriages. It dates the death to 1320, while srbija.gov.rs and Wikipedia give 1321. Commemoration (30 Oct) is one day after the death date, with no reason given. Text read by curl plus HTML stripping; the WebFetch summary was only a cross-check.

ref: Government of Serbia, Kosovo-Metohija portal, English page on King Milutin (section on Banjska monastery and cult), id 16240
quote_en: «In 1324, soon after his death in 1321, Milutin was sainted, and indispensable cult works were written for the purpose – service and eulogy.» Also: «He had to give her away to Milutin, although she was still only a child.»
edition: Official Serbian government web page (English), no print edition; read 18 Oct 2026
what_it_says: The page dates his formal veneration ('sainted') to 1324, soon after a death it dates to 1321, and says the cult texts (service and eulogy) were written for that purpose; the Vita of Milutin by Archbishop Danilo II is also dated to 1324 on the same page. It describes Simonida as 'still only a child' when given to Milutin.
limits: A state portal, not a Church or scholarly source, and it cites no document for the 1324 date. It gives no month or day for any act of canonisation and no description of its procedure. The death year 1321 conflicts with OCA and OrthodoxWiki (1320). The phrase 'sainted' may refer to local veneration rather than a synodal act; this page does not say.

claim: (e)/(f) Church opposition to the marriage; Simonida's later life; date of death
ref: Wikipedia (English), 'Simonida' (Simonida Nemanjić, born Simonis Palaiologina), section 'Life'; cites Fine 1994 (University of Michigan Press reprint of The Late Medieval Balkans)
quote_en: «Church circles in Constantinople opposed the marriage, but the emperor was determined to push the deal through, and in late 1298 he sent his trusted minister Theodore Metochites to Serbia to conduct the negotiations.» And: «The marriage was celebrated in Thessalonica in spring 1299, and the couple departed for Serbia in April.»
edition: Wikipedia, read 18 Oct 2026 (CC BY-SA; short quotations)
what_it_says: Says the Church circles in Constantinople opposed the marriage, that the emperor pushed it through, and that the wedding was in Thessalonica in spring 1299. It says she was born c. 1294 in Constantinople (so about 4-5 in 1299) and was the 'fifth wife'. It also says Milutin 'divorced his fourth wife, Ana Terter' to make way for her.
limits: Wikipedia, not a primary source. It does NOT name the patriarch as the opponent, and the article's body says nothing about the Church's conflict after the ceremony. Death date is internally inconsistent: 'c. 1294 - after 1336' in the lead vs 'Died after 1345' in the infobox. The article has no text on monastic life; the only trace is the category '14th-century Byzantine nuns' (a category, not a claim in the text). Its divorce-of-Anna-Terter statement conflicts with the Byzantine 'fourth wife' count in Fine/Kaldellis.

claim: (c) Church law on third and fourth marriages (logic of the reply: Church rules restricted such marriages)
ref: Basil of Caesarea, Canonical Letter to Amphilochius (Letter CLXXXVIII), canon IV; Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, vol. 8 (Schaff, public domain)
quote_en: «IV. In the case of trigamy and polygamy they laid down the same rule, in proportion, as in the case of digamy; namely one year for digamy (some authorities say two years); for trigamy men are separated for three and often for four years; but this is no longer described as marriage at all, but as polygamy; nay rather as limited fornication.»
edition: NPNF2 vol. VIII (1894, public domain), translation by Schaff's series; read on tertullian.org 18 Oct 2026
what_it_says: Basil's canon IV says that a third marriage (trigamy) brought penance of several years, and that a third or further marriage 'is no longer described as marriage at all'. It is penitential and says nothing about age.
limits: Penitential canon from the 4th century; it concerns repeat marriage, not age. The NPNF translation is 1894 (public domain); Greek not checked. Basil's own wording is not the same as the Rudder numbering used by later canonists.

claim: (c) 'Fourth marriage' canon: Basil's canon on polygamy and its later reading as a fourth marriage
ref: (a) Basil, Canonical Letter CCXVII (NPNF2 vol. 8), canon LXXX; (b) NPNF2 vol. 8 editor's footnote numbered 24 on the footnote page (footnote text as printed; attachment to canon LXXX not certain)
quote_en: (a) «LXXX. On polygamy the Fathers are silent, as being brutish and altogether inhuman. The sin seems to me worse than fornication. It is therefore reasonable that such sinners should be subject to the canons; namely a year's weeping, three years kneeling and then reception.» (b) footnote: «Zonaras and Balsamon understand by polygamy a fourth marriage; trigamy being permitted (cf. Canon l. p. 240) though discouraged.» Footnote URL: https://tertullian.org/fathers2/NPNF2-08/footnote/fn52.htm
edition: NPNF2 vol. 8 (1894, public domain) with the Benedictine editors' notes as reprinted by Schaff
what_it_says: Basil's canon LXXX (NPNF numbering) is about polygamy and imposes penance. The editor's note says that Zonaras and Balsamon read 'polygamy' as a fourth marriage, and that a third marriage was permitted though discouraged; the Benedictine annotator disputes that reading. So the canon that the 'fourth marriage' rule rests on is a 12th-century commentators' reading, not Basil's own clear words.
limits: I did NOT open the Greek or the text of Basil's canon L/50 ('Canon l. p. 240' in the Benedictine numbering), so the claim 'fourth marriages were completely forbidden' (Fine) is only PARTLY checked. The footnote is numbered 24 in the NPNF2 footnote page; in that page the same note also contains a comment on canon 'standers', so the note's attachment to canon LXXX is NOT certain (the note-number 23 in the text falls after canon LXXX). Schaff's reprint of 1894 (public domain); numbering differs between Basil, Rudder and NPNF.
